items.title: A key limitation of Greece’s €3 billion Achilles’ Shield agreement with Israel is that Greece will not receive the source code for the command-and-control (C2) systems.  Moshe Pate…
items.summary_raw: A key limitation of Greece’s €3 billion Achilles’ Shield agreement with Israel is that Greece will not receive the source code for the command-and-control (C2) systems.  Moshe Patel, head of Israel’s Missile Defense Organization, said source-code access was not included in the licensing agreement, despite Athens’ interest in maintaining control over the software architecture of the new air-defense network.  Israel will instead provide ongoing support, maintenance and future technical assistance.   This means Greece will operate the Spyder, Barak MX and David’s Sling systems without full access to the underlying proprietary software controlling them.  Source: Kathimerini

items.summary_raw:
Researchers urge governments to help worst afflicted countries, such as Nigeria and Algeria, which rely on oil revenues for public services

Conflict, migration and economic upheaval will accompany the global move away from oil, unless governments act urgently to help the worst afflicted countries to cope, research has found.

Nigeria, Iran, Angola and Algeria are among the countries that will be severely affected, as they rely strongly on oil revenues for their government and provision of public services, but have little diversification and too little capital to cushion the blow.

As a nation, we are the inheritors of a great empire that once stretched across three continents.  We have historical ties and kinship relations with a very broad geography.  We know very well how important closer relations between societies and strengthening commercial and cultural ties are in today's world.  With this understanding, in our foreign policy, we are striving to advance our relations with all countries through an approach that places Türkiye and Türkiye's interests at the center.

items.summary_raw: Turkish President Erdogan:  Categorically, we harbor hostility toward no one. On the contrary, we want to continue on our path as an independent, stable and prosperous state in the difficult geography in which we find ourselves.  We will never allow this path to be blocked. Those who are disturbed by our country becoming stronger and by its efforts to establish peace and stability in its region cannot turn us back from our path.  Have no doubt: no one has the power to change the course of history. Türkiye will shake hands with its friends, embrace its relatives, and reunite with its brothers.  Those who are friends with Türkiye will win, while those who harbor hostility will lose.

items.summary_raw: Turkish President Erdogan:  I want to state this clearly and unequivocally once and for all: no one should mistake our dignified and composed stance for weakness or allow it to give rise to false hopes.  We will not sit in the stands and watch hostile moves aimed at encircling our country in our region.  Türkiye is not against any country, any society, or any faith or culture; nor could such a thing ever be contemplated.  However, Türkiye stands against every act of lawlessness, every injustice, every form of oppression, and every act of banditry, regardless of who commits it—and it will continue to do so.

items.summary_raw:
Global AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisis

The greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to “degrow” the economy and to curb the population. The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy.

Nowhere has the tension between this proposition and reality become more palpable during this sweltering summer than in the conversation over air conditioning.

items.title: Three-Day Mourning for Armed Forces – Who Were the Two Phantom Pilots and What Investigators Are Examining
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS. One day after the tragedy at Tanagra, the Hellenic Air Force is in deep mourning, while the investigation into the crash of the F-4E Phantom II has moved to the center of attention. The two pilots who lost their lives were Air Force officers Ioannis Blesias, 40, and Dimitrios Petrou, 37, both experienced aviators. The aircraft belonged to the 338 Squadron “Aris” of the 117 Combat Wing. The two pilots had more than 1,500 flight hours, according to information available so far. Defense Minister Nikos Dendias declared three days of mourning across the Armed Forces, from Saturday, September 5, through Monday, September 7, following the deaths of the two crew members. The special committee investigating the crash is now examining every available piece of evidence from the fatal flight. The material collected includes videos from the air show, television footage and videos recorded by members of the public, while recorded communications with the control tower are expected to be particularly important.

Scientists are trying to assess possible environmental fallout from Gaza’s destroyed wastewater infrastructure, the report said.

items.summary_raw: Visioner ‼️‼️🇨🇿 BIG | The Czech Republic is preparing for the possibility that Europe could once again face a prolonged, high-intensity war with Russia. Prague is increasingly treating deterrence not as a political slogan, but as a long-term national project built around stronger forces, modern technology and a society capable of functioning during a major security crisis.  Under a draft national defence strategy extending to 2045, Russia is identified as the country’s principal security threat and the Czech military is to be prepared for a sustained high-intensity conflict. Prague plans to strengthen its armed forces, introduce 24 F-35 fighters, modernize two brigades and expand space-based intelligence capabilities. By 2030, authorities also intend to establish a new system for preparing the population for crisis situations. Military service would remain voluntary in peacetime, while the state would gain greater ability to mobilize citizens with medical, technical and IT expertise if circumstances require it. items.title: Iraqis queue for fuel as regional war disrupts imports
items.summary_raw:
Iraqis queue for fuel as regional war disrupts imports

Drivers formed long lines outside fuel stations in Baghdad on Saturday as gasoline supplies dropped in Iraq due to import disruptions caused by the Middle East war.

Despite being OPEC's second-largest oil producer, Iraq imports oil derivatives because its refineries do not produce enough gasoline to meet domestic demand.

In recent weeks, as regional hostilities drag on, long queues have been appearing every few days, mostly outside government-run fuel stations in Baghdad and other provinces.

The oil ministry said Friday that "regional events and the ongoing conflict are causing logistical challenges to tanker traffic, delaying their arrival at Iraqi ports".

Reporting by AFP

items.summary_raw:
US, allies push IAEA board to report Iran to UN Security Council

The United States, Britain, France and Germany are seeking a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog's board next week reporting Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, according to diplomats and the proposed text seen by Reuters.

If passed, the resolution would follow up on one adopted on June 12 of last year declaring Iran in breach of its non-proliferation obligations for not fully cooperating with an investigation into uranium traces found at undeclared sites.

Israel started bombing Iran's nuclear facilities the next day, soon joined by the US Iran's uranium-enrichment plants were destroyed or badly damaged.

At least 24 million barrels of crude oil were exchanged during ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman on Friday, according to maritime tracking service, TankerTrackers 

In a post on X, TankerTrackers said: “We’ve now tagged 17 crude oil and gas (LNG & LPG) ship-to-ship transfers which took place yesterday (2026-09-04) in the Gulf of Oman. At least 24 million barrels were being exchanged.”

“We also identified many more oil-laden tankers waiting for a dance partner in those waters,” the post read. 

“It appears that the dance floor itself is the limitation. It's getting quite crowded and port services are kept busy around the clock to ensure smooth and safe transfers.”

According to BILD, the Alabuga complex in Tatarstan is adding new production areas, warehouses and transport infrastructure across more than 1,000 hectares. items.title: Trump Administration Pushes to Remove Tax Exemption for Private Colleges with DEI Policies
items.summary_raw:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is proposing a new rule that would strip private schools and colleges of their tax-exempt status if they provide targeted help to students based on their race, a significant escalation in the White House's campaign to eradicate diversity programs directed at Black, Hispanic and other minority students. The Treasury Department proposed the change Thursday in a new regulation that, if made final, would kick in after May 2027. The rule is broadly aimed at ending any policies or programs that help students because of their race, and it specifically says such benefits in admissions, scholarships and facilities “would be incompatible” with the rule. It’s the latest attempt by the Trump administration to pressure schools and colleges to weed out diversity, equity and inclusion policies that had become common before President Donald Trump returned to the White House with a promise to end them. Trump officials have used Civil Rights-era laws to unwind the policies, saying they discriminate against white and Asian American students.

items.summary_raw: Visioner BIG | 🇺🇸🇩🇪‼️‼️ A high-level U.S.-German defense meeting is finally set for September 15, with Boris Pistorius heading to Washington for talks with Pete Hegseth after the Pentagon chief declined to meet him earlier this year.  According to POLITICO, the meeting will coincide with Pistorius’ visit for the rollout of Germany’s first F-35 fighter jets. The agenda is expected to include the recent attempted Russian drone attack in Germany and the Pentagon’s ongoing review of the U.S. military presence in Europe. The talks come after relations deteriorated following President Trump’s May decision to withdraw 5,000 U.S. troops from Germany after Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized the American war with Iran.  The meeting will test whether Washington and Berlin can stabilize a defense relationship that has become increasingly strained just as Europe faces growing pressure from Russia. Germany is rearming rapidly and taking on a larger security role, but any further reduction of U.S. forces would accelerate the shift toward greater European responsibility for deterrence on NATO’s eastern flank. items.title: Minister tells Brits to stock up on days of supplies after ‘supersize’ El Niño warning
items.summary_raw:
Exclusive: Angela Eagle urges people to be ‘a bit more resilient’ as she tells UK citizens to plan for national emergencies

British people have been urged to have enough food and water on hand to survive a few days without power or water, as the UN said the El Niño climate phenomenon was “supersizing before our eyes”, exacerbating extreme weather events worldwide.

Forecasters say they are braced for the biggest El Niño in 1,000 years, bringing wildfires and floods to parts of the world, and the threat of a wet, stormy winter for the UK.

As the British government plans a campaign urging citizens to prepare for national emergencies, Angela Eagle told the Guardian the likelihood of a wild winter showed the importance of having supplies at home.

items.title: Russia's Alabuga drone factory in Tatarstan is expanding massively.   The complex, which produces Shahed-copy Geran-2 drones and decoys, has grown by over 1,000 hectares across mul…
items.summary_raw: Russia's Alabuga drone factory in Tatarstan is expanding massively.   The complex, which produces Shahed-copy Geran-2 drones and decoys, has grown by over 1,000 hectares across multiple construction phases in 2025–2026, with new workshops, warehouses, roads, and a separate 450-hectare site south of the highway.   Production has shifted from Iranian kits to largely localized manufacturing using Chinese components.   The workforce pipeline runs through an adjacent vocational college that has used students including minors on assembly lines, with dormitories being built for tens of thousands of workers from North Korea, Africa, Latin America, and reportedly occupied Ukrainian territories.   Counter-drone lattice towers are going up around key buildings after repeated Ukrainian long-range strikes.   The site is under U.S., EU, and UK sanctions but construction continues at pace.  Source: Bild

items.title: ‘Supersizing before our eyes’: UN warns of record El Niño approaching
items.summary_raw:
Event is likely to be largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into a world already in a climate crisis

The El Niño climate phenomenon is “supersizing before our eyes”, the UN has said. The event is near certain to shatter temperature records, according to the latest forecasts.

The El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere where temperatures are already rising rapidly due to global heating. The combination means 2027 is set to “blow apart” the record and be the hottest year ever recorded.

items.title: The place that never freezes: the Arctic habitat where global heating threatens more ice, not less
items.summary_raw:
The race to study the North Water between Canada and Greenland before it changes has led to a bold plan for an Inuit-run protected area

Electric-blue meltwater sprays up under Terry Noah’s snowmobile as he races across sea ice extending out from Canada’s northernmost public community: Grise Fiord in Nunavut, a hamlet of 144 people closer to Murmansk in Russia than the Canadian city of Toronto. The bay’s cliffs loom higher and higher like stone icebergs as he approaches his destination across the bay.

Noah pulls his sled carefully over a seal’s breathing hole, about the circumference of a basketball. Using a custom-made winch, he lowers a submersible instrument into the sea below the ice.

items.title: US Oil Giant Chevron Confirms It Will Expand Operations in Venezuela
items.summary_raw:
Oil giant Chevron confirmed that it will expand operations in Venezuela after President Donald Trump announced an ambitious deal to develop the nation’s oil reserves and give the Pentagon a stake in the profits. Chevron, the only U.S. oil company with a major presence in Venezuela, said Wednesday that it has been assigned additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt, where it has active operations. The company plans to invest more than $7 billion over the next five years, with the goal of more than doubling its current production to about 600,000 barrels a day. “Chevron’s history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential,” CEO Mike Wirth said in a prepared statement. Venezuela holds the world's largest proven reserves, totaling more than 303 billion barrels of crude oil, according to OPEC's 2025 Annual Statistical Bulletin. Saudi Arabia is a distant second with 267 billion barrels.

items.title: Pacific Island Nations Seek To Turn Geopolitics Into Funding To Offset Climate Change Harm
items.summary_raw:
KOROR, Palau (AP) — When stormy seas batter Melekeok state on Palau’s biggest island, the Pacific Ocean floods right into people’s homes. “We keep telling the legislature we need to move inward,” said Bol Sebalt, 43, who was born and raised on the low-lying beachfront. “But because of a shortage of funding we cannot.” The fate of Melekeok, a chiefdom of 300 people, is echoed by stories from many island nations in remote parts of the vast Pacific Ocean. Their leaders, gathered for a summit in Palau this week, are wrestling once more with the question of how tiny countries with little global power can use major polluters’ geopolitical interest in their region to secure a chance of survival. Some hope for funding to help them adapt to changes they can’t reverse. Sebalt, a legislative clerk, is also a trained volunteer for her local disaster readiness team, making her one of 200 people across the western Pacific country now prepared to shepherd their communities through events such as catastrophic typhoons that have struck before.

items.title: Patagonia sues Trump over slashing of protected areas in Utah

Patagonia, the outdoor clothing and gear company, has joined a lawsuit challenging Donald Trump’s decision to significantly reduce the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah, removing protections from nearly 3m acres.

In July, the president approved the reduction of the sites by 90%, clearing the way to open the land to oil and gas companies. He argued in his proclamations that doing so would allow lands to be “put to a higher-priority use” and that they contained critical minerals important to “resource independence …[and] national security”.

items.title: The Economist reports that Russia has significantly ramped up its production rate of ballistic missiles, and is now producing approximately 100 units per month, including Iskander-…
items.summary_raw: The Economist reports that Russia has significantly ramped up its production rate of ballistic missiles, and is now producing approximately 100 units per month, including Iskander-Ms and RM-48U modified S-400s.  Last month, Ukrainian intelligence estimated that Russia produced 65 Iskander-M ballistic missiles in July. If the Ukrainian intelligence and Economist figures are both correct, it would indicate Russia is producing around 35 RM-48U modified S-400 ballistic missiles per month.   When taking into account the new Kn-23 ballistic missiles delivered to Russia by North Korea, Russia now has the capacity to launch weekly medium-sized attacks on Kyiv (~15 missiles per attack) without ever decreasing their total missiles in reserve, while still retaining 40 additional newly-produced missiles, as well as all of their Kn-23 ballistic missiles for attacks on different targets.   For reference, in 2022, it was estimated by Ukrainian intelligence that Russia produced just 3 Iskander-Ms per month. They also did not have any RM-48U modified S-400 or Kn-23 ballistic missiles at this time.

Online prediction markets, saturated by money staked on sport, crypto and politics, have now set their sights on a promising new area of growth: betting on the future livability of the planet itself.

The rise of gamified predictions on the unfolding climate crisis, and shorter-term weather forecasts, has been underscored by a new deal that allows Kalshi, a leading online financial exchange, to access data from the Weather Company, owner of the Weather Channel, to verify weather-related betting outcomes.

items.title: Britain is OK with public ownership, but only by foreign powers. Why?
items.summary_raw:
Arthur Downing, author of Power and the People: A History of British Energy, says all-encompassing rapid transition will need a mutualised system

Have you ever wondered why it is that most houses in the UK are reliant on gas boilers? Not what’s stopping more people from replacing them with heat pumps, but instead why and how the gas boiler became so ubiquitous in the first place?

Arthur Downing, the author of the new book Power and the People: A History of British Energy, can tell you exactly why. “We only have boilers in our houses because of a state-owned enterprise that went into everybody’s home and installed natural gas-suitable appliances at no direct cost,” he says. The nationalised gas industry of the 1940s to the 1980s, which oversaw this huge project, was for three decades one of the “most dynamic, innovative, efficient industries in Britain”, Downing says. Yet few of us would use these terms to describe it as such now.

items.title: Wednesday briefing: ​What’s behind the global backlash against datacentres?
items.summary_raw:
In today’s newsletter: Communities from Scotland to India are pushing back against datacentres they feel have been forced upon them, warning they threaten energy supplies and the climate

Good morning. This summer, datacentres have become targets of resistance across the world. Ever since the arrival of ChatGPT, big tech has been lobbying for the creation of enormous new facilities. Many governments claim they’re essential in any country that wants to cash in on AI.

Campaigners argue datacentres drain resources and exacerbate the climate crisis. The Scottish National Party has backed a moratorium on new developments; so has the Greens. The boom has been immense, and so has the backlash. Today’s newsletter explains why.

items.title: Global heating will hit at least 1.8C, UN warns, and there are ‘no good outcomes’
items.summary_raw:
But scientists say the world could get back to 1.5C through deep, rapid emissions cuts and removing carbon from the atmosphere

Global heating will reach at least 1.8C under even the most optimistic future, well beyond the Paris agreement goal of 1.5C, according to a UN report that warns every fraction of temperature rise intensifies destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and island and coastal city submersion.

The report by the Nairobi-based UN Environment Programme confirmed overshooting the 1.5C goal inscribed in the landmark Paris agreement of 2015 was now “unavoidable” and, despite some progress in addressing the human-caused climate crisis driven by burning fossil fuels, likely in the next few years.

items.title: Oil Giant Chevron Is Expected To Announce It Will Expand Operations in Venezuela, US Official Says
items.summary_raw:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Oil giant Chevron is expected to soon announce it will expand operations in Venezuela, a U.S. official said Tuesday. The official, who briefed reporters on the expected announcement, said that the company’s officials and Energy Secretary Chris Wright are expected to visit Venezuela on Wednesday where the new investment will be formally unveiled. The official spoke under condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House for the call. Chevron is the second-largest U.S. oil company and the only one with a major presence in Venezuela. Chevron did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The announcement comes after the White House confirmed on Monday it is partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) as part of President Donald Trump ’s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry.
